questions.title: The single recording error that moves the mean further than the median
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.1 (concepts of population, sample, random sample, discrete and continuous data)
questions.subtopic: 4.1 Concepts of population, sample, random sample
questions.challenge_mechanism: The mean sits above the median because one value is an outlier, and removing it collapses the gap between the two averages.
questions.question: Nine masses, in grams, are recorded as $5$, $6$, $7$, $8$, $9$, $10$, $11$, $12$ and $40$. The values are treated as a sample from a larger population of recorded masses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a random sample in this context, and give one reason why a random sample is preferred to a convenience sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median of the nine recorded masses, and comment on what the comparison between them suggests about the shape of the distribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show, using the interquartile range, that the value $40$ is an outlier; you should state both quartiles and the boundary you use.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The value $40$ is found to be a recording error and is removed; determine the new mean and the new median, and explain why the median moves less than the mean.

questions.answer:
**(a)** A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection, independently of the others **(M1)**. The population here is every mass that could have been recorded, and a random sample would select nine items using a random generator **(A1)**. A convenience sample takes the items easiest to reach, so awkward items are excluded and the sample is not representative **(R1)**. That exclusion biases any estimate from the data, whereas random selection keeps the sample representative **(A1)**. Random selection makes the summary trustworthy.

**(b)** Adding the nine values gives $5+6+7+8+9+10+11+12+40=108$ **(M1)**, so the mean is $\frac{108}{9}=12$ **(A1)**. In order, the fifth value is $9$, so the median is $9$ **(A1)**. The mean lies above the median, suggesting a tail towards the larger values, because one large value lifts the mean without moving the middle **(R1)**. The comparison indicates skew.

**(c)** With nine ordered values the lower quartile is the mean of the second and third, $\frac{6+7}{2}=6.5$ **(M1)**, and the upper quartile is the mean of the seventh and eighth, $\frac{11+12}{2}=11.5$ **(A1)**. The interquartile range is $11.5-6.5=5$ **(A1)**. The upper boundary is $Q_3+1.5\times IQR=11.5+7.5=19$, and since $40>19$ the value $40$ is an outlier **(A1)(AG)**. The standard $1.5$ IQR rule places $40$ far outside this boundary.

**(d)** Removing $40$ leaves $n=8$ and a total of $108-40=68$ **(M1)**, so the new mean is $\frac{68}{8}=8.5$ **(A1)**. The new median is the mean of the fourth and fifth values, $\frac{8+9}{2}=8.5$ **(A1)**. The mean falls by $3.5$ while the median falls by only $0.5$, because the mean uses the size of every value and reacts to the outlier, while the median depends only on position **(R1)**. This difference separates the two averages.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the idea of equal chance of selection. The (A1) requires a concrete mechanism, such as numbering the items and using a random generator, applied to this context. The (R1) is for naming the bias that convenience sampling introduces, and the final (A1) for linking random selection to representativeness. A candidate who only defines a random sample without applying it to masses earns at most two marks.

(b) Award (M1) for the sum $108$, (A1) for the mean $12$, and (A1) for the median $9$. The (R1) requires a statement about skew or tail direction; merely saying the mean is larger earns nothing unless it is linked to the shape.

(c) The (M1) is for either quartile position; the (A1) requires both quartiles correct. The third (A1) is for the interquartile range $5$, and the final (A1)(AG) for the boundary $19$ together with the explicit comparison $40>19$. A candidate who quotes $19$ but never compares it with $40$ forfeits the last mark.

(d) Award (M1) for the reduced total, (A1) for the new mean, and (A1) for the new median. The (R1) is for the positional-versus-magnitude explanation. Follow through from an incorrect outlier decision is allowed, provided the arithmetic is consistent.
questions.explanation:
This item turns on the difference between two measures of centre when one value is wrong. The nine masses are deliberately almost symmetric, running from $5$ to $12$, so that the mean and median would agree at $8.5$ were it not for the final entry. That entry, $40$, is far larger than the rest and lifts the mean to $12$ while leaving the median at $9$. The gap of three grams is produced by one recording.

The intended route is to sum the values, divide by nine, order them and read off the fifth. Part (c) then applies the $1.5$ IQR rule, which is the only reason the value $40$ can be labelled an outlier rather than merely large. Candidates who compute the quartiles by splitting the ordered list into four equal groups often mishandle nine values, since the groups cannot be equal; the convention used here takes the median of each half, giving $6.5$ and $11.5$.

Part (d) turns the comparison into an argument. Removing $40$ gives a mean of $8.5$ and a median of $8.5$, so the two measures now coincide exactly. The reason the mean moved further is that it is computed from every value, so a single extreme observation carries weight, whereas the median is fixed by the position of the middle and only shifts when the count changes. The classic error is to remove the outlier and then recompute the median from the remaining eight values by taking the fourth alone; with an even count the median is the mean of the two central values, here $\frac{8+9}{2}=8.5$. A candidate who treats the outlier as genuine keeps the inflated mean and reaches the opposite conclusion about the shape.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.1 bullet on population, sample and random sample. The lever is a single extreme recording, 40, placed in an otherwise nearly symmetric list from 5 to 12; those values were chosen so that the mean is lifted to 12 while the median stays at 9, so that the 1.5 IQR rule gives an upper fence of exactly 19 and therefore makes 40 an outlier beyond doubt, and so that removing it brings both averages to the same value 8.5. The item is not a reskin because the outlier is used twice: once to motivate the random-sample discussion and once to force an explanation of why the two measures of centre respond differently to the same deletion.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the sum 108, the mean 12, the median 9, the quartiles 6.5 and 11.5, the interquartile range 5, the upper fence 19 and the comparison 40 > 19, together with the reduced total 68 and the new mean and median 8.5.

questions.title: Why the tallest bar is not the most crowded class
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.2 (presentation of data: frequency distributions, histograms, cumulative frequency, box-and-whisker plots)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The class with the largest frequency is not the class with the greatest density once unequal widths are rescaled, and the median must be interpolated rather than read off.
questions.question: One hundred observations are grouped into five classes of unequal width. The classes and their frequencies are $0\le x<2$ with frequency $12$, $2\le x<4$ with frequency $8$, $4\le x<8$ with frequency $40$, $8\le x<12$ with frequency $24$, and $12\le x<20$ with frequency $16$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why frequency alone cannot be plotted on the vertical axis when the class widths differ, and calculate the frequency density of each of the five classes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the median lies in the class $4\le x<8$, and estimate its value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the interquartile range, showing clearly the positions you use.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Estimate the 90th percentile and interpret it in the context of the observations.

questions.answer:
**(a)** With unequal widths a tall bar shows a wide class, not a crowded one, so the axis must show frequency per unit of width **(M1)**. Frequency density is frequency divided by class width, so the five densities are $\frac{12}{2}=6$ **(A1)**, $\frac{8}{2}=4$ and $\frac{40}{4}=10$ **(A1)**, then $\frac{24}{4}=6$ and $\frac{16}{8}=2$ **(A1)**. The tallest bar is the class $4\le x<8$, with density $10$, although its width is only four. Density, not frequency, is comparable across unequal widths.

**(b)** The total frequency is $100$, so the median is at position $50$ **(M1)**. The cumulative frequencies are $12$, $20$, $60$, $84$ and $100$, so the fiftieth value falls in the class $4\le x<8$ **(A1)**. Within that class, $30$ of the $40$ observations are needed **(M1)**, so the median is $4+\frac{30}{40}\times 4=7$ **(A1)**. This assumes an even spread in the class.

**(c)** The lower quartile lies at position $25$ **(M1)**. The cumulative frequency reaches $20$ at $x=4$, so $5$ more come from the class of width $4$, giving $Q_1=4+\frac{5}{40}\times 4=4.5$ **(A1)**. The upper quartile lies at position $75$, and the cumulative frequency reaches $60$ at $x=8$, so $Q_3=8+\frac{15}{24}\times 4=10.5$ **(A1)**. The interquartile range is $10.5-4.5=6$ **(A1)**. Each quartile uses the same interpolation as the median.

**(d)** The ninetieth percentile lies at position $90$ **(M1)**. The cumulative frequency reaches $84$ at $x=12$, so $6$ observations come from the class $12\le x<20$ of width $8$ and frequency $16$, giving $P_{90}=12+\frac{6}{16}\times 8=15$ **(A1)(A1)**. In context, about ninety per cent lie below $15$, so ten per cent exceed it **(A1)**. The value is an estimate, again assuming an even spread in the top class.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the idea that unequal widths require a density rather than a frequency. The three (A1) marks are for the five densities, grouped so that any three correct values earn two marks and all five earn three; accept the densities written as fractions. A candidate who plots frequencies forfeits the reasoning mark but may still earn the (A1) marks for the numbers.

(b) Award (M1) for locating position $50$, (A1) for identifying the class $4\le x<8$, (M1) for the interpolation fraction, and (A1) for the value $7$. A candidate who reads $7$ directly from the cumulative curve earns the same marks, provided the position is stated.

(c) The (M1) is for the position $25$; the (A1) is for $4.5$. The second (A1) is for $10.5$, and the final (A1) for the interquartile range $6$. Follow through from an incorrect $Q_1$ or $Q_3$ is allowed when the subtraction is consistent.

(d) The (M1) is for the position $90$ and (A1)(A1) for the interpolation and the value $15$. The final (A1) is for a contextual interpretation in terms of the proportion above or below $15$; a bare number without context does not earn it.
questions.explanation:
The item turns on frequency and frequency density answering different questions. The class $4\le x<8$ contains the largest frequency, $40$, but a narrower class can be equally crowded per unit of width: the class $0\le x<2$ has density $6$, against $10$ for the wide class. A candidate who simply plots the frequencies produces a histogram whose areas no longer represent the data, because a bar of height $40$ over a width of four claims an area of $160$ observations. The densities $6$, $4$, $10$, $6$ and $2$ restore the property that each area equals the frequency it represents.

The cumulative frequencies are needed for the median and the quartiles, and the key step is to convert a position into an interpolation within a class. For the median the position is $50$, which lies in the third class; the fraction is $\frac{50-20}{40}$, and multiplying by the class width of four gives an addition of three, so the median is $7$. The quartiles use positions $25$ and $75$ in the same way, and the percentile uses position $90$.

The common error is to assume that the median is the midpoint of the class containing it, which would give $6$ and is wrong because the observations are not evenly distributed within the class boundary. Another error is to use cumulative frequencies rather than positions, or to take $Q_3$ from the fourth class when the cumulative frequency of $75$ still lies in the third. The class limits were chosen so that each interpolation fraction is simple: $\frac{30}{40}$, $\frac{5}{40}$, $\frac{15}{24}$ and $\frac{6}{16}$ all reduce to tidy quarters or eighths, so a correct method produces exact values while a mistaken one usually does not.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.2 bullet on frequency distributions and cumulative frequency. The lever is a set of five classes of unequal width, 2, 2, 4, 4 and 8, with frequencies 12, 8, 40, 24 and 16; those numbers were chosen so that the total is exactly 100, so that the frequency densities are 6, 4, 10, 6 and 2, and so that every interpolation fraction reduces to a simple quarter or eighth, giving the exact median 7, quartiles 4.5 and 10.5 and ninetieth percentile 15. The item is not a reskin because the unequal widths are the subject of the first part and every later estimate depends on interpolating within a class rather than reading a value from a boundary.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the total frequency 100, the five frequency densities 6, 4, 10, 6 and 2, the cumulative frequencies, and the interpolated median 7, lower quartile 4.5, upper quartile 10.5, interquartile range 6 and ninetieth percentile 15.

questions.title: The coding that leaves the mean alone but doubles the spread
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.3 (measures of central tendency and dispersion; effect of constant changes to the data)
questions.subtopic: 4.3 Measures of central tendency and dispersion
questions.challenge_mechanism: Two data sets share an identical mean while one has double the standard deviation, and the coding rule must be inverted rather than reapplied.
questions.question: The data set $A$ is $\{4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$, and the set $B$ is obtained from $A$ by the coding $b=2a-6$. In the final parts a different set $x$ is coded as $w=1.5x-4$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the set $A$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the mean and the standard deviation of the coded values $2a-6$, and explain why the mean changes by the whole transformation while the standard deviation is affected only by the multiplicative part.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A different set $x$ is coded as $w=1.5x-4$, and the coded values have mean $14$ and standard deviation $4.5$. Find the mean and the standard deviation of $x$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why subtracting $4$ leaves the standard deviation unchanged while multiplying by $1.5$ multiplies it, and give one reason a researcher might code data.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The mean of $A$ is $\frac{4+5+6+7+8}{5}=6$ **(M1)(A1)**. The deviations from the mean are $-2$, $-1$, $0$, $1$ and $2$, whose squares are $4$, $1$, $0$, $1$ and $4$ **(M1)**. The variance is $\frac{10}{5}=2$, so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{2}=1.41$ to three significant figures **(A1)**. The divisor is $5$ because these values are treated as the whole population.

**(b)** Coding with $b=2a-6$ gives $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$ and $10$, whose mean is $\frac{30}{5}=6$ **(M1)(A1)**. The deviations are doubled, so each squared deviation is multiplied by $4$ and the variance becomes $4\times 2=8$ **(M1)**, giving a standard deviation of $\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}=2.83$ **(A1)**. The mean changes by the whole transformation because every value is shifted and scaled, while the standard deviation ignores the shift of $-6$ and is scaled only by the factor $2$.

**(c)** Since the coding is $w=1.5x-4$, the mean satisfies $14=1.5\bar{x}-4$ **(M1)**, so $1.5\bar{x}=18$ and $\bar{x}=12$ **(A1)**. The standard deviation is unaffected by the subtraction of $4$, so $4.5=1.5\sigma_x$ **(M1)**, giving $\sigma_x=\frac{4.5}{1.5}=3$ **(A1)**. The inverse transformation is obtained by solving the coding rule rather than applying it again.

**(d)** Subtracting $4$ translates every value by the same amount, so all deviations from the mean are unchanged and the standard deviation is unchanged **(M1)(A1)**. Multiplying by $1.5$ scales every deviation by $1.5$, so the variance is multiplied by $1.5^2$ and the standard deviation by $1.5$ **(A1)**. A researcher might code data to remove an awkward constant, such as a large offset, so that the numbers are easier to handle later **(R1)**. Only the multiplicative part of the coding changes the spread.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the sum and (A1) for the mean $6$. The second (M1) is for the squared deviations, which may be listed rather than summed. The (A1) is for the variance $2$ or the standard deviation $\sqrt{2}$; accept $1.41$ but do not accept a standard deviation quoted without the variance shown.

(b) The (M1)(A1) pair is for the coded values and their mean $6$. The second (M1) is for recognising that the variance is multiplied by $4$, and the final (A1) for $2\sqrt{2}$. A candidate who recomputes from the coded list earns full credit, but the explanation must still refer to the multiplier.

(c) The (M1) is for forming $14=1.5\bar{x}-4$, and the (A1) for $\bar{x}=12$. The second (M1) is for $4.5=1.5\sigma_x$, with the final (A1) for $\sigma_x=3$. Follow through from an incorrect coding equation is allowed if the algebra is consistent.

(d) The (M1)(A1) pair is for the translation argument, and the (A1) for the scaling of the standard deviation by $1.5$. The (R1) is for any valid reason for coding, such as simplifying large or awkward numbers. A candidate who claims the subtraction changes the spread forfeits the reasoning mark.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the algebra of constant changes to a data set. For set $A$ the mean is $6$ and the variance is $2$. Coding by $b=2a-6$ produces the set $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$, $10$, which has the same mean of $6$ but a variance of $8$. The two sets therefore sit at exactly the same place on the number line while the second is visibly more spread out, which is the contrast the title names.

The intended route separates the two parts of a linear coding. A shift of $-6$ moves every value by the same amount, so every deviation from the mean is unchanged and the standard deviation is untouched. A multiplier of $2$ scales every deviation by $2$, so each squared deviation is scaled by $4$ and the variance by $4$; the standard deviation, being a square root, is scaled by $2$ alone. This is why $\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$.

Part (c) reverses the direction. Given the coded mean $14$ and the coded standard deviation $4.5$, the candidate must solve $14=1.5\bar{x}-4$ and $4.5=1.5\sigma_x$, obtaining $12$ and $3$. The common error is to apply the coding rule again rather than invert it, which produces a mean of $17$ instead of $12$. A second error is to divide by $1.5^2$ rather than $1.5$ when recovering the standard deviation, confusing variance with standard deviation. The numbers were chosen so that the coded mean equals the original mean, which disguises the shift, and so that the inverse values are whole numbers.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.3 bullet on measures of central tendency and dispersion and the effect of constant changes to the data. The lever is a coding b = 2a - 6 applied to the set 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; those numbers were chosen so that the coded set is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, which shares the mean 6 with the original while doubling the variance from 2 to 8 and the standard deviation from sqrt 2 to 2 sqrt 2, and so that the inverse problem w = 1.5x - 4 recovers the whole numbers 12 and 3. The item is not a reskin because the coding must be inverted rather than reapplied, and because the invariance of the mean under a zero-sum shift is made the explicit object of the explanation.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the mean 6 and variance 2 of A, the standard deviation sqrt 2, the coded set 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with mean 6 and variance 8, the standard deviation 2 sqrt 2, and the inverse coding giving mean 12 and standard deviation 3.

questions.title: A correlation of 0.8 that licenses no claim of cause
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.4 (linear correlation of bivariate data; Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient r)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The summary statistics hide the sample size and the causal trap, so a correct r must be paired with an explicit refusal to infer causation.
questions.question: Ten paired observations $(x,y)$ are summarised by $\sum x=60$, $\sum y=90$, $\sum x^{2}=400$, $\sum y^{2}=900$ and $\sum xy=588$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $S_{xx}=40$ and $S_{yy}=90$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate $S_{xy}$ and hence the product-moment correlation coefficient $r$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Interpret $r$ in context, calculate the coefficient of determination, and comment on what it measures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student claims that because $r$ is close to $1$, an increase in $x$ causes an increase in $y$; explain why that conclusion does not follow from $r$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The corrected sums are $S_{xx}=\sum x^{2}-\frac{(\sum x)^{2}}{n}=400-\frac{60^{2}}{10}$ **(M1)** $=400-360=40$ **(A1)**. Similarly $S_{yy}=\sum y^{2}-\frac{(\sum y)^{2}}{n}=900-\frac{90^{2}}{10}$ **(M1)** $=900-810=90$ **(A1)(AG)**. Both subtract the part of the sum of squares explained by the mean, leaving the variation about the mean.

**(b)** The cross term is $S_{xy}=\sum xy-\frac{(\sum x)(\sum y)}{n}=588-\frac{60\times 90}{10}$ **(M1)** $=588-540=48$ **(A1)**. Hence $r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}=\frac{48}{\sqrt{40\times 90}}$ **(M1)** $=\frac{48}{\sqrt{3600}}=\frac{48}{60}=0.8$ **(A1)**. The denominator is the geometric mean of the two variations, so $r$ measures the shared variation.

**(c)** The value $r=0.8$ indicates a strong positive linear relationship between $x$ and $y$, meaning that larger values of $x$ tend to accompany larger values of $y$ **(A1)**. The coefficient of determination is $r^{2}=0.64$ **(M1)(A1)**, so about $64$ per cent of the variation in $y$ is accounted for by the linear relationship with $x$. It measures the strength of the linear association only, not the agreement between the variables **(R1)**. A high $r^{2}$ does not show that the linear model is the right one.

**(d)** A correlation coefficient measures association within the observed data and cannot establish direction or cause **(M1)**. An increase in $y$ could cause an increase in $x$, or a third variable could drive both, so the relationship is symmetric in $x$ and $y$ and the roles can be exchanged without changing $r$ **(A1)(A1)**. The correlation also depends on the range of values sampled and says nothing about values outside that range **(R1)**. Causation requires additional evidence, such as a controlled experiment or a plausible mechanism.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for the corrected-sum-of-squares form and (A1) for $S_{xx}=40$; the second (M1)(A1) pair is for $S_{yy}=90$. Accept the equivalent expressions $\sum(x-\bar{x})^2$. A candidate who uses $n-1$ rather than $n$ in the correction term should be corrected, since the formula uses the mean of the sample.

(b) The (M1) is for $S_{xy}$ in corrected form and the (A1) for $48$. The second (M1) is for the correlation formula, and the (A1) for $0.8$. A candidate who reaches $0.8$ from a correct formula earns full credit even if $S_{xx}$ or $S_{yy}$ were slightly wrong, provided the follow-through is consistent.

(c) The first (A1) is for a contextual interpretation of $r$. The (M1)(A1) pair is for $r^{2}=0.64$, and the (R1) is for stating that $r^{2}$ measures linear association only. A bare percentage without context does not earn the (R1).

(d) The (M1) is for recognising that correlation does not determine direction. The (A1)(A1) marks are for the reverse-direction possibility and for a confounding variable. The (R1) is for a valid statement about the need for further evidence. Reject any answer that simply asserts correlation is not causation without applying it to this data.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the product-moment correlation coefficient and on what it does not license. The summary statistics are given in raw form, so the first task is to convert them into the corrected sums of squares. The sample size is ten, and the corrections subtract $\frac{60^{2}}{10}=360$ and $\frac{90^{2}}{10}=810$, leaving $S_{xx}=40$ and $S_{yy}=90$. These values are the variation about the mean in each variable, and the cross term $S_{xy}=48$ measures how much of that variation is shared.

The coefficient is then $\frac{48}{\sqrt{3600}}=\frac{48}{60}=0.8$, a value that most candidates will recognise as strong. The square, $0.64$, is the coefficient of determination and is the quantity that carries a percentage interpretation. The trap is the final part, where a student treats a large $r$ as evidence of cause. Correlation is symmetric: exchanging $x$ and $y$ leaves $r$ unchanged, so the data alone cannot tell which variable, if either, drives the other.

The common errors are to use $n-1$ in the correction term, which changes both $S_{xx}$ and $S_{yy}$ and destroys the exact value $0.8$, and to interpret $r^{2}$ as the proportion of points lying on the line. The numbers were chosen so that the denominator is exactly $60$ and the coefficient is exactly $0.8$, and so that the sample size is hidden inside the corrections rather than stated in the summaries. A candidate who notices that $r$ is unchanged when the roles of $x$ and $y$ are exchanged has the cleanest argument against causation.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.4 bullet on linear correlation and Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient. The lever is the raw summary form: the ten pairs are given only through sums of x, y, x squared, y squared and xy, so the sample size must be recovered from the problem statement before any correction can be applied. The numbers 60, 90, 400, 900 and 588 were chosen so that Sxx = 40, Syy = 90 and Sxy = 48, giving the exact denominator sqrt 3600 = 60 and therefore the exact coefficient 0.8, and so that the causal trap in the final part can be answered without any further arithmetic. The item is not a reskin because the correlation is paired with an explicit refusal to infer causation, and because the hidden sample size is part of the reasoning rather than a stated quantity.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently: the corrected sums Sxx = 40, Syy = 90 and Sxy = 48, the denominator sqrt 3600 = 60, the coefficient 0.8, the coefficient of determination 0.64, and the means 6 and 9.

questions.title: Six outcomes, three questions, and the effect of replacement
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.5 (concepts of trial, outcome, equally likely outcomes, sample space and event)
questions.subtopic: 4.5 Concepts of trial, outcome, equally likely outcomes, sample space
questions.challenge_mechanism: The sample space is small enough to enumerate but the conditional phrasing hides which outcomes qualify, and replacement rebuilds the space entirely.
questions.question: Two different numbers are chosen at random from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. In the final part the two numbers are chosen with replacement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the sample space of all pairs of different numbers, and state the number of equally likely outcomes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the larger of the two numbers is exactly $3$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the larger number is at least $3$ and the smaller number is odd.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The two numbers are now chosen with replacement; determine the probability that the two numbers are equal, and explain how the sample space changes.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Choosing two different numbers from four gives $\binom{4}{2}=6$ pairs, namely $\{1,2\}$, $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{2,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ **(M1)(A1)**. Because each pair is equally likely and order does not matter, each outcome has probability $\frac{1}{6}$ **(A1)**. The sample space therefore contains six equally likely outcomes, and every event can be counted directly from this list **(A1)**. The unordered convention avoids counting each pair twice.

**(b)** The larger number is exactly $3$ in the pairs $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ **(M1)(A1)**. There are two such outcomes out of six, so the probability is $\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$ **(A1)**. The outcome $\{3,4\}$ is excluded because its larger number is $4$, not $3$ **(R1)**. The count is a direct enumeration, so no multiplication rule is needed.

**(c)** The condition requires the larger number to be at least $3$ and the smaller number to be odd. The qualifying pairs are $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ **(M1)(A1)**, giving three outcomes out of six, so the probability is $\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$ **(A1)**. The pair $\{2,3\}$ fails because its smaller number, $2$, is even **(R1)**. Checking each pair against both conditions is the only reliable way to count this event.

**(d)** With replacement each of the two choices is made from four numbers, giving $4\times 4=16$ equally likely ordered outcomes **(M1)(A1)**. The two numbers are equal in the four outcomes $(1,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,3)$ and $(4,4)$, so the probability is $\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}$ **(A1)**. The space now contains ordered pairs and repeated values, so it is larger and its outcomes are different from before **(R1)**. Replacement is what makes the two choices independent.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) Award (M1) for recognising the count $\binom{4}{2}$ or for listing pairs systematically, and (A1) for all six pairs. The second (A1) is for the probability $\frac{1}{6}$, and the final (A1) for stating that the outcomes are equally likely. A candidate who lists ordered pairs must still identify the six unordered outcomes.

(b) The (M1) is for identifying the outcomes whose larger member is $3$, and the (A1) for the pair $\{1,3\}$ or $\{2,3\}$. The final (A1) requires both pairs and the value $\frac{1}{3}$. The (R1) is for explaining the exclusion of $\{3,4\}$; a candidate who counts three favourable outcomes earns at most one mark.

(c) The (M1)(A1) pair is for the qualifying pairs $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. The (A1) is for $\frac{1}{2}$. The (R1) is for testing at least one excluded pair against both conditions, such as $\{2,3\}$ failing the odd condition.

(d) Award (M1) for the product $4\times 4$, and (A1) for the sixteen ordered outcomes. The (A1) is for the four equal pairs and the probability $\frac{1}{4}$, and the (R1) for describing how replacement changes the sample space. Follow through from part (a) is allowed.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the concepts of trial, outcome, sample space and event, and it uses a space small enough to enumerate but phrased so that careless counting fails. Two different numbers are chosen from four, giving six unordered pairs. The sample space is fixed and finite, and each outcome is equally likely, so every probability in the first three parts is a simple ratio of counts.

The first subtlety is that the pairs are unordered. If a candidate lists ordered pairs there are twelve, and each has probability $\frac{1}{12}$; the probabilities are unchanged, but the counts double and the arithmetic must be adjusted. The convention should be stated before counting begins, because mixing the two conventions is the most common source of error.

Part (b) asks for the larger number to be exactly three, which is true of $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,3\}$ only. Part (c) adds a second condition, that the smaller number is odd, and the qualifying pairs are $\{1,3\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. The pair $\{2,3\}$ looks promising because its larger number is three, but its smaller number is even, so it is excluded. This is the conditional phrasing that hides the answer: a candidate who counts only on the larger number obtains the wrong event.

Part (d) changes the trial by allowing replacement. The sample space becomes the sixteen ordered pairs, repeated values are now possible, and the event that the two numbers are equal has probability $\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}$. The numbers were chosen so that the probabilities are the simple fractions $\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{1}{3}$, $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$, and so that the excluded pair in part (c) is genuinely tempting. Replacement is the lever that rebuilds the space.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.5 bullet on trial, outcome, equally likely outcomes, sample space and event. The lever is a two-stage choice from the set 1, 2, 3, 4 with the two numbers required to be different; those values were chosen so that the sample space has exactly six unordered pairs and the probabilities come out as the simple fractions one sixth, one third, one half and one quarter, and so that the pair 2 and 3 is a genuine distractor in the conditional part because its larger member is three while its smaller member is even. The item is not a reskin because replacement rebuilds the sample space from six unordered pairs into sixteen ordered pairs, and the change in the space is the explicit subject of the final part.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently by enumerating the six unordered pairs and the sixteen ordered pairs with replacement: the counts one, two and three favourable outcomes, the probabilities one sixth, one third and one half, and the four equal pairs giving one quarter.
